Your agent paid $4,200 instead of $420 — and the test scored it a perfect 1.00. Here's why, and it isn't a bug in the agent. 👇 Tool correctness checks that an agent called the right tools: you author the tools you expect, run the agent, compare what it called. By default, it compares tool names. Only the names. So the golden says "call make_payment." The agent calls make_payment — with an amount ten times too high. The names match. Score: 1.00. That extra zero never enters the math. For a lookup tool, matching on name is fine. For make_payment, bind_policy, file_claim — the arguments ARE the behavior. A right-tool, wrong-amount call is the whole risk, and name-matching waves it through. The fix isn't clever: assert the arguments, not just the name. Author the expected parameters on the golden, and $4,200 vs $420 fails like it should. A tool call is a verb and its objects. Grade only the verb and you haven't graded the call. Chains
Using an LLM in isolation is fine for simple applications, but more complex applications
require chaining LLMs — either with each other or with other components.

LangChain provides the Chain interface for such “chained” applications. We define a
Chain very generically as a sequence of calls to components, which can include other
chains.

In the sample project explained in this article, the Sequential Chain is used which will

Because it is all in writing before you shop, you know exactly what you are agreeing to and can factor it into your numbers from day one.

Does it matter if a buyer's agent works full time or part time?

It can matter a lot. A full time agent is available when a new listing hits, when a counteroffer needs a fast answer, and when an inspection issue pops up on a weekday afternoon. On Staten Island good homes move quickly, so an agent who can drop everything to get you in the door gives you a real edge. I have been full time for nearly a decade, and that availability is a big part of why my buyers win.
